description: Somos un equipo de estudiantes de media superior y técnicos en programación con un enfoque fuerte en el aprendizaje, buscamos aprender, pero desarrollar algo con un alto valor que pueda ser utilizado de verdad.
summary: Much of the scientific information about our planet is communicated through visual representations and technical language, making it difficult to understand for people with visual impairments and for children who are still building their scientific knowledge. This limits the opportunities for many people to explore, understand, and become aware of the changes the Earth is undergoing. Our project responds to NASA’s The Earth Information Jukebox challenge, which seeks to broaden access to scientific information about our planet through sonification. We developed KASAMA for Earth, a multisensory, inclusive, and educational website that turns elements of NASA’s scientific visualizations into sound experiences, complementing visual information with sounds that represent the data so users can explore, interpret, and understand environmental phenomena from an auditory perspective. Our goal is to foster understanding, awareness, and reflection about the changes our planet is experiencing, sparking curiosity about environmental phenomena and helping people learn about their causes, understand their consequences, and recognize their impact on our surroundings. We also want to promote awareness of our responsibility to protect the planet. Because each person learns, interprets, and relates to information differently, accessibility is at the core of our approach: everyone, regardless of their needs, should be able to access scientific information and understand it properly.
details:
A NOTE ON BROWSERS

Please open the site in Google Chrome, Microsoft Edge or Safari on a computer. Voice control uses the browser's own speech recognition, and those are the browsers where it works: Firefox does not have it, and Brave switches it off for privacy…

WHAT IT DOES

KASAMA for Earth is an interactive web jukebox that turns NASA Earth visualizations into music, so anyone can hear what our planet looks like. The visitor picks one of eight "records" (Climate Time Machine, ocean currents, lightning from space, forest height, sea surface temperature, water vapour, carbon dioxide, and smoke, dust and haze), watches it wrapped on a 3D globe, and plays it on a DJ-style mixer. Live: https://kasamaforearth.work

HOW IT WORKS

1.⁠ ⁠Data pipeline (Python). Scripts download frames from the NASA Scientific Visualization Studio and world maps from NASA GIBS, and reduce every frame to a small set of numbers: brightness, contrast, saturation, fine detail, bright spots, a 12-bin colour histogram, and a 4 x 8 grid of cells. The result is static JSON, so the site needs no server.

2.⁠ ⁠Picture-to-sound rules (TypeScript). Every frame lasts one bar of 8 steps and feeds three voices:

•⁠ ⁠Chord, from colours: the most common hue gives the root note along the circle of fifths; warm colours play major, cool colours play minor.

•⁠ ⁠Melody, from light: the grid is scanned left to right, one column per step. The brightest cell sings; higher in the picture means a higher register, and dark columns are rests.

•⁠ ⁠Sparkles, from spots that stand out: they fall on the columns where one cell stands out most (a lightning flash, a city, a plume).

Nothing is random: the same picture always plays the same music.

3.⁠ ⁠Climate Time Machine. Here the grid holds the data itself: land temperature projections from NASA NEX-GDDP-CMIP6, 1950 to 2100, under four emissions scenarios (SSP1-2.6, SSP2-4.5, SSP3-7.0, SSP5-8.5). The hottest land cell of each column sings, and its note climbs with how much that place has warmed since 1950. As the planet heats up, the root note rises, the harmony turns minor and a dissonant note appears. The Emissions fader switches scenario, and both the map and the music change.

4.⁠ ⁠Sound changes the picture. The note that is sounding lights up its cell on the globe, muted voices lose their marks, and the listener can focus the music on one of 11 world zones. The picture never shows invented effects, only real data.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

•⁠ ⁠Accessibility: blind and low-vision visitors can explore Earth data by ear. The page has a spoken tutorial, a narrator that reads every control, full keyboard control, and voice control (hold the space bar and speak).

•⁠ ⁠Education: kids mode uses simpler words and twelve missions, such as "Choose a cooler future".

•⁠ ⁠Context: four voiced stories of real events (Hurricane Otis 2023, the Pakistan floods of 2022, the Amazon drought of 2023, and 2024 as the first year above 1.5 °C), in the language of the place and in English, plus climate news by region.

•⁠ ⁠Climate awareness: hearing the same year under low and very high emissions makes the difference between futures immediate.

TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGY

•⁠ ⁠Front end: TypeScript, React 19, Vite.

•⁠ ⁠Sound: Tone.js (Web Audio API), with one channel per voice, faders, mute, solo, DJ filter and reverb.

•⁠ ⁠3D globe: Three.js with React Three Fiber.

•⁠ ⁠Voice: Web Speech API for recognition and as fallback speech; narrator and story clips recorded once with ElevenLabs (AI-generated voices).

•⁠ ⁠Data pipeline: Python 3 with NumPy, Pillow, Requests and ffmpeg.

•⁠ ⁠Hosting: GitHub Pages; GitHub Actions rebuilds the site and refreshes the news every six hours.

•⁠ ⁠Data: NASA SVS, NASA NEX-GDDP-CMIP6, NASA GIBS (GEDI, GHRSST MUR, AMSR2, MERRA-2), Copernicus CAMS for the carbon dioxide map, and NASA Earth Observatory and Google News RSS for headlines.

CREATIVITY

Instead of adding a soundtrack to the images, the images write the music through fixed, explainable rules, and each rule can be heard on its own with Solo. The interface is a mixer, so exploring data feels like playing an instrument, and the controls are named after what they read in the data (Colours, Light, Bright spots; Heat, Warming, Hot spots in the Time Machine).

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

•⁠ ⁠Honesty: every record is labelled Measured, Model + measurements, Forecast model or Projection. The heat index is computed by us from the colours of NASA's frames; it is consistent with the data but is not an official figure in degrees.

•⁠ ⁠Clarity: every note can be traced back to a cell of the picture.

•⁠ ⁠Inclusion: light and dark themes, reduced motion, screen-reader labels, and a narrator that is off by default so it does not talk over VoiceOver or NVDA.

•⁠ ⁠Openness: static site, open data, public code at https://github.com/MarcoT007/the-earth-jukebox-kasama-developing-solutions-v2
